title: Most of a Jet Engine's Thrust Never Touches the Fire

sources: Bypass ratio about 10:1 (for every unit of air through the core, about ten go around it): GE Aerospace, GE9X product page, 'approximate 10:1 bypass ratio'. https://www.geaerospace.com/commercial/engines/ge9x
Fan diameter 134 in (3.4 m), shown on screen: GE Aerospace, GE9X product page. https://www.geaerospace.com/commercial/engines/ge9x

Bypass flow generates up to 80 percent of the thrust; bypass ratio up to 12:1 on the most advanced turbofans; fuel-air mixture burns at approximately 1,700 degrees Celsius: MTU Aero Engines, AEROREPORT 'How does a turbofan engine work?'. https://aeroreport.de/en/good-to-know/how-does-a-turbofan-engine-work

80-90 percent of the air drawn in by the fan is exhausted through the fan nozzle and provides most of the engine's thrust; combustor exhaust passes through the turbine, which turns the shaft driving the fan and compressor: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2016), Commercial Aircraft Propulsion and Energy Systems Research, ch. 2. https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/23490/chapter/6

A turbofan generates more thrust for nearly the same fuel used by the core, and turbofans are more fuel efficient than basic turbojets ('thirsty' turbojet); fan air goes around the core like air through a propeller: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics, Turbofan Thrust. https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/BGP/aturbf.html

Turbojets produce high-velocity hot exhaust jets at takeoff and were noisy; turbofans reduced noise by lowering jet exhaust velocity ('loud' turbojet): Huff and Envia, NASA Glenn, 'Jet Engine Noise Generation, Prediction and Control' (2004). https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20050198876
